# Missing Data

::: {.callout-note title="Learning Goals" collapse="false"}
After this lesson, you should be able to:

* Explain why the cause of missingness in a dataset matters
* Explain the differences between data MCAR, MAR, and MNAR
* Describe some R packages for exploring and handling missing data
* Visualize missing data to identify patterns
* Explain what complete- and available-case analysis are
* Explain what single and multiple imputation are
* Use the mice package to perform multiple imputation on a dataset
:::

:::{.callout-important title="Required Packages"}
This chapter uses the following R packages:

* ggplot2
* mice
* naniar

For a refresher about how to install and load packages, see the
[Packages][r-basics-packages] section of DataLab's R Basics workshop reader.

[r-basics-packages]: https://ucdavisdatalab.github.io/dwr_workshop_r_basics/chapters/getting-started/getting-started.html#sec-packages
:::

We say that data are **missing** or **incomplete** when some measurements are
deliberately left out or left unspecified in a dataset. Just a few examples of
why data might be missing are:

* Measurement tools sometimes produce measurements that are too inaccurate to
  report directly or are obviously incorrect. In some cases, a tool might not
  be working at all at the moment it's needed.
* In survey studies, participants might skip or decline to answer some of the
  questions. Similarly, in medical studies, some participants might decide to
  drop out.
* In time-limited studies, the study might end before data can be collected for
  all subjects. For instance, at the end of a 1-year study of lightbulb
  lifespans, it's possible that some bulbs will still be working; the exact
  lifespan of those bulbs is unknown.

When data are missing, we have less information to use in analyses, so our
conclusions are always weaker than they would've been with complete data.
Certain kinds of missing data also interfere with how well a sample represents
the population from which it was drawn, leading to inaccurate or biased results
from standard statistical methods.

This chapter introduces a few general-purpose ways to think about, summarize,
identify patterns in, and statistically account for missing data. Most of the
methods described in this chapter assume that we have no information about the
values of the missing data; for cases where we there is partial information,
see @sec-censored-data.


## Why Data Are Missing {#sec-why-data-are-missing}

The reasons *why* data are missing are the key to determining how they'll
impact statistical methods.

As a demonstration of this idea, consider a study of sea lion growth where the
researchers weigh each of the sea lions in the study. Suppose their scale
occasionally malfunctions and displays "ERROR" instead of a weight, so some of
the sea lion weights are missing. Assuming the scale malfunctions randomly and
independently of which sea lion is being weighed, we have no reason to expect
that the observed weights and the censored weights are distributed differently.
If we simply ignore the missing weights and proceed with a statistical
analysis, our conclusions might be limited by lack of data, but they will still
accurately (up to sampling error) reflect the population of sea lions.

On the other hand, suppose that the researchers' scale only malfunctions and
displays "ERROR" for especially heavy sea lions. Then the observed weights will
mostly be from light sea lions and the missing weights will mostly be from
heavy sea lions. If we ignore the missing weights and proceed with a
statistical analysis, we'll likely underestimate the typical weight of a sea
lion, and other analyses may also be inaccurate. The reasons why the weights
are missing matter for subsequent statistical work.

@little2019 divide reasons for missingness into three categories based on how
they affect subsequent analyses (from least to most severe):

* Data are **missing completely at random** (**MCAR**) when the probability of
  being missing is equal across all observations, regardless of the measured
  value and of other features. In the sea lions example, weights from the scale
  that occasionally malfunctions randomly and independently are MCAR.

  For data MCAR, simple methods for handling missing data are generally safe to
  use and yield accurate results.

* Data are **missing at random** (**MAR**) when the probability of being
  missing is equal across observations *after grouping by (or controlling for)
  other features in the dataset*. That is, missingness depends on other
  features, but they're recorded in the dataset. In the sea lions example, the
  weights would be MAR if the scale malfunctions more for certain researchers,
  and the dataset indicates which researcher recorded each weight.

  For data MAR, we must account for the cause when we handle the missing data.
  Simple methods may yield inaccurate or biased results.

* Data are **missing not at random** (**MNAR**) when the probability of being
  missing is unequal across observations even after controlling for other
  features in the dataset. In other words, the missingness is due to unknown,
  external features or due to the measured values. In the sea lions example,
  weights from the scale that malfunctions more for heavy sea lions are MNAR.
  Older texts sometimes refer to MNAR as "not missing at random" (NMAR).

  Censored data, which are the subject of @sec-censored-data, are an example of
  MNAR data where the probability of being missing is 100% for measured values
  in specific known intervals.

Unfortunately, there's no statistical procedure to determine whether data are
MNAR. This is inherent in what MNAR means: the cause of missingness is
unknown---it's the values of the missing data themselves or something that
isn't measured in the dataset. To conclude whether data are MNAR, we need a
thorough understanding of how the data were collected.

Even for datasets where we're confident (or comfortable assuming) that data are
MCAR or MAR, statistical methods can't tell us which is the case with complete
certainty. There are some statistical tests we can apply, but like all
statistical tests, these are subject to error.

:::{.callout-warning}
*How many data are missing* is another important detail to consider before,
during, and after analysis. Even when a dataset is structurally large (hundreds
of rows and columns, for instance), if most of the data are missing, the
information content can still be low.

Regardless of why data are missing, extreme lack of data leads to low-quality
estimates (where the error is mostly due to sampling variation rather than
bias in MCAR and some MAR scenarios).
:::

<!--
  For data MCAR, it's safe to remove all incomplete observations (observations
  where at least one feature is missing) and then proceed with analysis; this
  is called **complete-case analysis**. The main shortcoming of complete-case
  analysis is that it wastes data, because incomplete observations might only
  be missing data for a few features. More elaborate methods for handling
  missing data don't have this problem, but sometimes simplicity is worth
  sacrificing some data.

  For data MAR, complete-case analysis may lead to inaccurate or biased
  results, but there are other methods we can turn to instead.
-->


## Missing Data in R

R provides built-in support for missing data through the special value `NA`. It
also provides functions to detect missing data (such as `is.na`) and parameters
to ignore missing data (`na.rm` for most statistical functions).

There are many packages that extend R's missing data capabilities. These three
packages provide functions to clean, explore, and visualize missing data:

* The [naniar][] package (see the [online documentation][naniar-docs]
* The [VIM][] package (after installing, see `?VIM`)
* The [tidyr][] package (see the [online documentation][tidyr-docs])

[naniar]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.naniar
[naniar-docs]: https://naniar.njtierney.com/
[VIM]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.VIM
[tidyr]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.tidyr
[tidyr-docs]: https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/

The naniar and VIM packages provide roughly similar functionality. The tidyr
package is specifically focused on cleaning data (and not just missing data).

Most standard statistical methods require complete data. In order to accomodate
missing data, we have two options:

* Discard the observations with missing data;
* Use a statistical model (such as a linear model) to fill the missing data
  with estimates.

For the latter, we recommend the popular [mice][] package (which has [online
documentation][mice-docs]); @sec-statistics-with-missing-data explains more
about why we recommend this package. The associated [ggmice][] package provides
supplementary functions to make ggplot2 plots.

[mice]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.mice
[mice-docs]: https://amices.org/
[ggmice]: https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.ggmice

In this reader, we use naniar for exploration and mice for filling missing
data.

:::{.callout-note title="See Also"}
The [CRAN Task View: Missing Data][cran-na] page is a curated list of R's most
widely-used packages related to missing data.

[cran-na]: https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/MissingData.html

The website [R-miss-tastic][r-miss] describes missing data workflows and
packages for R (and to a lesser extent, Python). It also lists learning
materials such as lectures, books, and example datasets. It's updated
regularly.

[r-miss]: https://rmisstastic.netlify.app/
:::


## Dataset: CA Least Terns

For the examples in this chapter, we'll use the California least terns dataset.
@sec-ca-least-terns describes the dataset in more detail.

:::{.callout-important}
[Click here][ca-least-tern] to download the 2000-2023 California least terns
dataset.

[ca-least-tern]: https://ucdavis.box.com/s/m2w5l2ebp2rey2do5lnn38y1e3u31pin

If you haven't already, we recommend you create a directory for this workshop.
In your workshop directory, create a `data/` subdirectory. Download and save
the dataset in the `data/` subdirectory.
:::

The structure of the dataset is:

```{r}
terns = read.csv("data/2000-2023_ca_least_tern.csv")
str(terns)
```

The structural summary alone shows that there are missing data.

We can use R's built-in `is.na` and `colSums` functions to compute counts of
missing values per column:

```{r}
colSums(is.na(terns))
```


## Visualizing Missing Data {#sec-visualizing-missing-data}

When we explore a dataset with missingness, the goal is generally to understand
how missing data within each feature are distributed relative to other
features. In other words, we want to identify patterns and relationships. This
kind of exploration is often helpful for distinguishing between data MCAR and
MAR (@sec-why-data-are-missing), although it can't tell us whether the data are
MNAR. Exploring the missing data can also help us identify other limitations
and potential problems, such as lack of sufficient data.

The key to exploring missing data is to create a **shadow dataset**, where each
feature is replaced with a binary or categorical shadow feature that indicates
missingess. We can do this on a per-column basis with R's built-in `is.na`
function. After constructing the shadow dataset, we can use standard
exploration methods for categorical data (such as those in
@sec-categorical-features) to explore missingess.

Visualizations are a great way to explore data even when the data are missing.
We can use the naniar package to produce several useful visualizations of
missingness; the package is convenient because most of its functions compute
the shadow dataset for us automatically.

Let's use the California least terns dataset to demonstrate some of the missing
data visualizations naniar provides. First, the `vis_miss` function makes a
plot that summarizes missingness for an entire data frame:

```{r}
#| label: fig-terns-missing
#| fig-cap: >
#|    At-a-glance plot of missingness in the California least terns dataset.
library("naniar")

vis_miss(terns)
```

Rows are represented by horizontal lines with a segment for each column. The
lines are stacked vertically, matching the layout of rows in the data frame.
Gray segments indicate observed data, while black segments indicate missing
data. This way we can see which columns have missing data, how much data are
missing, and where missing data co-occur.

@fig-terns-missing shows that most of the features in the dataset are complete.
There's a small proportion (about 2\%) of missing observations in the `bp_`,
`fl_`, and `total_nests` features. There are slightly more (about 30\%) in the
`nonpred_` features. The most dramatic missingness (about 93\%) is in the
`pred_` and `total_` (excluding `total_nests`) features, with a high degree of
co-occurrence across these features.

An **upset plot** is another way to visualize co-occurrence of missing values.
Upset plots are general-purpose plots for visualizing set intersections, but
the naniar package uses them specifically to visualize missingness.

We can make an upset plot with the `gg_miss_upset` function. The `nsets`
parameter controls how many features are shown. The `nintersects` parameter
controls how many co-occurrences (across collections of two or more features)
are shown:

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-terns-upset
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Upset plot of missingness in the California least terns dataset.
gg_miss_upset(terns, nsets = 20, nintersects = 15)
```

The small horizontal bar plot on the left shows the number of missing data for
each feature. The large vertical bar plot on the right shows the number of
missing data co-occuring across each collection of features. Each collection of
features is indicated below the vertical bar plot; a black dot means the
feature is included in the collection. The function automatically selects the
feature collections with the most co-occurrences.

@fig-terns-upset provides additional information about the co-occurrences in
the `pred_` and `total_` features: there are 477 co-occurrences across only
those features, and there are another 134 across those features as well as the
`nonpred_` features. There are lower numbers of co-occurrences across other
collections of features.

Another way to look for missing data patterns is to group with a categorical
feature and then examine missingness within each group. This is especially
helpful for checking whether data are MAR according to a particular categorical
feature. The naniar package provides the `gg_miss_fct` function to plot
missing data by group. The first argument should be the dataset, and the second
argument should be the feature to group by:

```{r}
#| label: fig-terns-time-na
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Plot of missingness grouped by year for the California least terns
#|    dataset.
gg_miss_fct(terns, year)
```

The plot shows the groups along the x-axis and each feature in the dataset
along the y-axis. The proportion of missing values in each (group, feature)
combination is represented by a shaded rectangle. In this case, lighter colors
indicate more missing data.

Based on @fig-terns-time-na, the `pred_` and `total_` features are entirely
missing from 2007 onwards. For other features with missing data, most of them
are before 2016 or 2017.

Scatter plots are enormously useful for investigating relationships between
features. When the features have missing data, we can still make a scatter plot
by simply discarding the observations where either feature is missing. This
allows us to see relationships in the observed data, but can also be misleading
because it makes it easy to forget about the missing data entirely. The naniar
package's `geom_miss_point` is an alternative to `geom_point` that makes a
scatter plot with the missing data shown. The missing data are represented by
jittered points that lie well outside the range of the observed data; they're
also color-coded. Let's make a scatter plot of `total_nests` versus `fl_min`,
with missing data shown:

```{r}
#| label: fig-terns-scatter-na
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Scatter plot of total nests versus minimum fledglings for the California
#|    least terns dataset.
library("ggplot2")

ggplot(terns) +
  aes(x = total_nests, y = fl_min) +
  geom_miss_point(shape = "o")
```

@fig-terns-scatter-na shows that for this pair of features, there are only a
few missing values (about 5-20) relative to observed values (hundreds).

In this section we've highlighted some of the most useful plots the naniar
package provides, but see the [reference][naniar-viz] for a complete list. The
package also provides functions for exploring without visualizing (for
instance, by making tables) and for filling missing data.

[naniar-viz]: https://naniar.njtierney.com/reference/index.html#visualisation


## Statistics with Missing Data {#sec-statistics-with-missing-data}

Most statistical methods assume that all data are observed. For example, it's
unclear how to compute a sample mean when data are missing. In order to use
these methods, we must modify the dataset so that there aren't any missing
data. We can do this either by discarding observations with missing data or by
filling in the missing data.

First, let's consider two common ways to discard observations:

* In **complete-case analysis**, we discard every observation with missing data
  in *any* feature. Then we proceed with analysis.

  The main advantage of complete-case analysis is its simplicity: special
  statistical methods are not necessary. The main disadvantage is that it
  wastes information---the incomplete observations may contain a lot of
  observed data.

  Complete-case analysis is safe when data are MCAR. When data are MAR or MNAR,
  complete-case analysis can bias results.

* In **available-case analysis**, we discard incomplete observations separately
  for each method based on the features that are needed. This means that we may
  use a different number of observations in each estimate or model!

  The main advantage of available-case analysis is that it uses data more
  efficiently than complete-case analysis. The main disadvantage is that
  comparing or combining results where the number of observations differs is
  challenging, and some statistics---such as correlation---depend on being able
  to do so.

  Available-case analysis is safe when data are MCAR. When data are MAR or
  MNAR, available-case analysis can bias results.

Now we turn to ways to **impute**, or fill in, missing data. The fundamental
idea is to use a statistical model fitted on the observed data to predict the
missing data. The model can be simple, such as computing a sample mean, or
something more complicated. We'll consider just two of many options for
imputing missing data:

* Sample means: for each feature, replace missing data with the mean of the
  observed data.

  This is a poor way to impute data. The main advantage is that it's simple and
  leads to unbiased estimates of means for data MCAR. The main disadvantage is
  that it biases most other statistics, regardless of why data are missing. As
  a specific example, it artificially lowers variance in the dataset, which
  leads to standard error estimates that are too small. Avoid using this
  approach.

* Linear models: for each feature, fit a linear model on the observed data with
  the feature as a response and other features as predictors. Replace missing
  data with predictions from the model.

  The main advantage of imputing with linear models is that it leads to
  unbiased estimates of means (and the model coefficients) for data MAR,
  provided that the features which influence missingness are included in the
  models. The main disadvantage is that it biases most other statistics. For
  instance, it leads to correlation estimates that are too large and standard
  error estimates that are too small. This approach is better than using sample
  means, but still leaves a lot to be desired.

Before we learn about a better way to impute missing data, let's try sample
mean imputation on the California least terns dataset in order to demonstrate
why it's problematic. We'll impute two features, `total_nests` and `fl_min`,
which each have a relatively small proportion of missing data (see
@fig-terns-missing).

Before we impute, let's construct shadow features to help us mark the imputed
data on a plot later:

```{r}
terns$na_total_nests = is.na(terns$total_nests)
terns$na_fl_min = is.na(terns$fl_min)
```

Now we can replace the missing data in `total_nests` and `fl_min` with the
respective means of the features:

```{r}
imp_mean = terns

imp_mean$total_nests[terns$na_total_nests] =
  mean(terns$total_nests, na.rm = TRUE)
imp_mean$fl_min[terns$na_fl_min] =
  mean(terns$fl_min, na.rm = TRUE)
```

To see why sample mean imputation is often a poor choice, let's make a scatter
plot of `total_nests` versus `fl_min`. We'll use the shadow features to
color-code the imputed data and visually de-emphasize the observed data (via
transparency):

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-terns-imputed-mean
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Scatter plot of total nests versus minimum fledglings for the California
#|    least terns dataset, with missing data replaced by sample means.
ggplot(imp_mean) +
  aes(
    x = total_nests,
    y = fl_min,
    color = na_total_nests | na_fl_min,
    alpha = na_total_nests | na_fl_min
  ) +
  geom_point(shape = "o") +
  scale_alpha_discrete(range = c(0.4, 0.8)) +
  lims(x = c(0, 250), y = c(0, 250)) +
  labs(color = "Imputed", alpha = "Imputed")
```

In @fig-terns-imputed-mean, notice that all of the imputed data lie on a
horizontal line at the mean of `fl_min`. It's difficult to see, but the
rightmost imputed point is actually several points, all with the same
coordinates. Compared to the observed data, variation in the imputed data is
much smaller. The imputed data also deviate from the fan-shaped pattern in the
observed data. For these features, the proportions of missing data were low, so
the effect of imputing on subsequent analyses will be small. However, for
features with more missing data, it could be substantial and lead to incorrect
results.

After discarding or imputing missing data, we can use standard statistical
methods, such as linear models:

```{r}
fit = lm(fl_min ~ total_nests, imp_mean)
summary(fit)
```


### Multiple Imputation

Complete-case analysis is simple, but wastes data and only works well when data
are MCAR. Available-case analysis makes it difficult to combine statistics for
multiple features (and is also limited to data MCAR). Imputation with sample
means or predictions from linear models tend to bias subsequent analyses. We
need a better way to handle missing data.

Donald Rubin gets to the root of the problem with all of the techniques we've
seen so far:

> Imputing one value for a missing datum cannot be correct in general, because
> we don’t know what value to impute with certainty (if we did, it wouldn’t be
> missing).

This insight led Rubin and others to develop **multiple imputation**. The
central idea of multiple imputation is to impute by creating multiple copies of
the original dataset, where the imputed values are different in each copy. We
then conduct statistical analyses on each copy. When we're finished, we combine
the results from all of the copies using two formulas known as **Rubin's
rules**.

:::{.callout-note title="Note: Single Imputation"}
**Single imputation** refers to imputation techniques that only produce one
dataset, such as those described at the beginning of
@sec-statistics-with-missing-data.
:::

Within the multiple imputation procedure, we can use any model we want to
impute values for each copy of the dataset. We'll generally chose models that
include some randomness, so that we can simulate the randomness when making
predictions and thus get different imputed values for each copy. For instance,
we can use a linear model where we combine the predictions with simulated or
sampled residuals.

Multiple imputation generally leads to unbiased statistics for data MCAR and
MAR. When data are MNAR, the results can still be biased.

:::{.callout-note title="Note: Sensitivity Analysis"}
When we suspect data are MNAR, a common two-step approach is to:

1. Conduct an analysis as if the data are MAR (or MCAR).
2. Conduct a sensitivity analysis that examines hypothetical "what-if"
   scenarios for the missing data, measuring how (and how much) the results of
   the step 1 analysis change.

Qualify the results and conclusions from the step 1 analysis with the results
from the sensitivity analysis.
:::

Several R packages implement multiple imputation, but [mice][] (which stands
for "multiple imputation by chained equations") is the most widely-used
package. The package provides functions that automate most of the steps in
multiple imputation.

The package's `mice` function performs multiple imputation. The first argument
must be the original dataset. The parameter `m` controls the number of copies.
The parameter `method` controls which model is used to generate predictions
(see `?mice` for a complete list).

Let's compute multiple imputations for the California least terns dataset.
We'll make just 3 copies of the dataset. We'll use the `norm` method, which
fits a different linear model on each copy and uses it to make a prediction
with a randomly sampled residual:

```{r}
#| warning: false
library("mice")

imp = mice(terns, m = 3, method = "norm", printFlag = FALSE)
```

The mice package's `complete` function provides access to the copies of the
dataset. Let's make a scatter plot of `total_nests` versus `fl_min` for each
copy, with the imputed data marked (similar to @fig-terns-scatter-na):

```{r}
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-terns-scatter-mi
#| fig-cap: >
#|    Scatter plots of total nests versus minimum fledglings for the California
#|    least terns dataset, for each copy generated by multiple imputation.
#|    In each plot, imputed data are marked.
ggplot(complete(imp, "long")) +
  aes(
    x = total_nests,
    y = fl_min,
    color = na_total_nests | na_fl_min,
    alpha = na_total_nests | na_fl_min
  ) +
  geom_point(shape = "o") +
  scale_alpha_discrete(range = c(0.4, 0.8)) +
  lims(x = c(0, 250), y = c(0, 250)) +
  labs(color = "Imputed", alpha = "Imputed") +
  facet_wrap(vars(.imp))
```

The mice package provides a modified version of R's built-in `with` function to
make conducting analyses on all copies of a multiply imputed dataset
convenient. For instance, this code fits a linear model with outcome `fl_min`
and predictor `total_nests` on each copy:

```{r}
fits = with(imp, lm(fl_min ~ total_nests))
```

The package's `pool` function uses Rubin's rules to combine results from
multiple copies of a multiply imputed dataset. This code computes the final
estimates from the fitted linear models:

```{r}
summary(pool(fits))
```

For these features, the results are almost the same as when we used sample mean
imputation (@sec-statistics-with-missing-data). This is because the proportion
of missing data is very low; we would see a more dramatic difference if the
proportion was higher.

:::{.callout-note title="See Also"}
_Statistical Analysis with Missing Data_ [@little2019] is a definitive textbook
about missing data. The authors provide detailed explanations of most methods
in use today (some of which they created).

_Handbook of Missing Data Methodology_ [@molenberghs2014] is an anthology
similar in scope and depth to @little2019. It's an excellent companion or
alternative to that book.

[_Flexible Imptuation of Missing Data_][flex] [@van_buuren2021] was written by
the creator of the mice package for R and provides some examples of how to use
the package. The first chapter is an excellent, intuitive overview of missing
data concepts and methods.

[flex]: https://stefvanbuuren.name/fimd/

All three books include graduate-level mathematics, which can make for
difficult reading. Unfortunately, we're not aware of any missing data books
that provide a gentler introduction to the subject (but see
[R-miss-tastic][r-miss], which is regularly updated, for many more references).
:::
